direct_answer:
BASF states it has a Group-wide compliance management system and Compliance Program designed to prevent compliance violations (including corruption) from the outset, supported by continuous systematic compliance risk analyses (including corruption) at divisional and Group company level, targeted local/unit-specific requirements, and regular compliance audits by the internal Corporate Audit unit that monitors adherence to guidelines and the effectiveness of the compliance management system [Source 3][Source 14][Source 8]. BASF identifies procurement as the function most at risk for corruption and bribery and applies a “Zero Gift Policy” prohibiting procurement employees from accepting gifts of any kind [Source 3]. BASF operates a publicly accessible Compliance Hotline (available to employees and external parties) and records reports in a global compliance case management system; it investigates suspected misconduct and can implement countermeasures such as improved controls, additional training/information, updates to internal regulations, and disciplinary measures up to termination of employment [Source 2][Source 1]. BASF also states it prohibits retaliation against good-faith reporters and bases its procedures on applicable whistleblower-protection legal guidelines [Source 12]. Training-wise, BASF provides workshops and mandatory training (basic/refresher/specialized) that includes corruption and bribery content and information about grievance mechanisms; refresher training is repeated every two years; in 2024, more than 120,000 employees received over 105,000 hours of Code of Conduct training, and BASF states that functions-at-risk are fully covered by the training program [Source 13].

Regarding incidents/legal proceedings: BASF discloses that in the reporting year there were no convictions for violations of anticorruption and antibribery regulations [Source 8]. The provided passages do not state the number/nature of confirmed corruption incidents, any fines, or details of any corruption-related legal proceedings during the reporting period beyond the statement of no convictions [Source 8].
compliance_rationale: The passages provide substantial description of prevention/detection elements (risk analyses, audits, hotline/case management, non-retaliation, training, identification of at-risk function and zero-gift rule) and a clear statement that there were no convictions for anti-corruption/anti-bribery violations in the reporting year [Source 3][Source 2][Source 12][Source 13][Source 8]. However, key ESRS G1-3 and G1-4 specifics are not evidenced in the retrieved text (e.g., investigator independence from management chain, formal reporting of outcomes to governance bodies, quantitative training coverage for at-risk functions and for administrative/management/supervisory bodies, and quantified confirmed incidents/fines/legal cases), limiting full compliance.
disclosure_gaps: Procedures for investigating corruption/bribery allegations: whether investigators/investigating committee are separate from the management chain involved (independence) is not evidenced in the provided passages (ESRS G1-3(b)).
Process for reporting investigation outcomes to administrative, management and supervisory bodies is not evidenced (ESRS G1-3(c)).

How anti-corruption/anti-bribery policies are communicated to relevant persons to ensure accessibility and understanding is only partially evidenced (internal platforms/online Code of Conduct), but not specifically tied to all relevant persons including external stakeholders beyond the hotline (ESRS G1-3(e)) [Source 13][Source 1].

Training metrics required by ESRS: percentage of functions-at-risk covered (quantified) and extent of training for administrative, management and supervisory bodies are not quantified; only a qualitative statement that functions-at-risk are fully covered and that certain leader trainings were offered (ESRS G1-3(f)) [Source 13].
Confirmed incidents of corruption or bribery: total number and nature of confirmed incidents (if any) is not disclosed in the provided passages (ESRS G1-4).
Fines/amounts for violations of anti-corruption and anti-bribery laws are not disclosed; only 'no convictions' is stated (ESRS G1-4(a)) [Source 8].

Public legal cases/proceedings related to corruption or bribery and their outcomes during the reporting period are not disclosed in the provided passages (ESRS G1-4, optional but relevant to the question).

Actions taken to address breaches specifically related to corruption/bribery procedures/standards are not separately disclosed (only general countermeasures for Code of Conduct cases) (ESRS G1-4(b)) [Source 2].
key_findings: BASF’s compliance management system aims to prevent violations (including corruption) through continuous systematic risk analyses and targeted requirements; procurement is identified as most at risk, with a 'Zero Gift Policy' for procurement employees [Source 3].

BASF uses a publicly accessible Compliance Hotline and a global compliance case management system; all suspected misconduct is investigated and may lead to controls/training/regulatory updates/disciplinary measures, including terminations [Source 2][Source 1].
BASF states it prohibits retaliation against good-faith reporters and aligns procedures with whistleblower-protection legal guidelines [Source 12].

BASF provides ongoing mandatory compliance training (including corruption/bribery content); refresher training every two years; in 2024, >120,000 employees received >105,000 hours of Code of Conduct training; functions-at-risk are stated to be fully covered [Source 13].
BASF reports no convictions for violations of anti-corruption and anti-bribery regulations in the reporting year [Source 8].
